outcome: As of the most recent sources found, Legendre's conjecture is still unproven and unresolved. Since 26 January 2024 the bearing events are: a February 2026 review and RH-conditional progress on the weaker question of primes between consecutive larger powers (not the conjecture itself); an October/November 2025 unreviewed Russian-language preprint claiming a proof (not yet read by me); and a 2025 computational verification to a finite bound (which settles no instance of the universal claim). No AI-attributed mathematics on this problem has been found so far. Search is incomplete (see `incomplete`).
problem_asks: For every positive integer n, there is a prime p with n^2 < p < (n+1)^2. One universal claim over n ≥ 1 (the statement says 'every positive integer n'). Its quantities: (a) the existence of a prime strictly inside each interval (n^2, (n+1)^2); (b) that this holds for all n, not for a range of n. Wikipedia's January 2024 wording is 'for every positive integer n, there is a prime between n^2 and (n+1)^2'. Nothing else is asked.

events.what_happened: Marc Chamberland and Armin Straub, 'Weakening the Legendre Conjecture', arXiv:2602.22502 (math.NT), a review of Legendre's conjecture and of recent progress on the weaker question of primes between consecutive larger powers x^(2+δ) and (x+1)^(2+δ). Abstract: 'Here, we review Legendre's conjecture on primes between consecutive squares and recent progress on the weaker question of primes between consecutive larger powers.'
events.revisions: Only v1 listed on the abstract page (submitted Thu, 26 Feb 2026, 13 KB, 14 pages).
events.delivers: Does not prove Legendre's conjecture (δ = 0). Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, combines a result of Carneiro, Milinovich and Soundararajan with a large-scale computation by Sorenson and Webster to get primes between x^(2+δ) and (x+1)^(2+δ) for all real x ≥ 1 when δ ≥ 1/4. For smaller δ > 0 it gives an explicit x0(δ) such that such primes exist for x ≥ x0. These are results on a weaker, exponent-changed question, conditional on RH.
events.remains: The whole of problem_asks: the case δ = 0 (primes between consecutive squares, n^2 and (n+1)^2) is untouched, and the result is conditional on RH.
events.time_since_posted: about 7.5 months at 12 October 2026, from the arXiv v1 date; no later engagement searched yet
events.direction: Neutral toward the conjecture. It treats Legendre's conjecture as an open conjecture ('a conjecture ... every interval between consecutive squares contains a prime', per the 2026 paper summary) and adds conditional progress on a weaker question. It does not cut for or against the δ = 0 claim.

events.what_happened: Vladimir Trushnikov (author 'TrushnikovVV'), a preprint on preprints.ru (files/2520 and files/2382), in Russian with an English abstract, which a search summary describes as claiming a proof of Legendre's conjecture by comparing gaps between primes with gaps between consecutive squares. I could not read the text: the fetched PDF gave only metadata and a Visio-export structure, and I did not obtain the abstract or argument.
events.revisions: Unknown. The search summary says October 2025; the fetched file metadata says created and modified 2025-11-23. The two dates conflict and I cannot pin the month, so the day/month is left out.
events.delivers: Claimed (per the search summary, unverified): a proof of Legendre's conjecture for all n. Not checked by me.
events.remains: Unknown until the text is read; if the claim holds, nothing remains.
events.time_since_posted: about 11 to 12 months; no engagement found by my searches so far
events.doubts: Not peer-reviewed; posted on preprints.ru, which does not review; the author's standing in analytic number theory is not established; the argument has not been read by me, so no specific error is identified; the preprint's text could not be extracted, so I cannot say whether the argument is complete. Record as a reason to doubt only what is verified: none yet.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture (cuts for the conjecture), if the search summary is accurate.

events.what_happened: M. Sundarakannan, 'Existence of primes between two consecutive squares', arXiv:1908.08995 (2019). A search summary says it asserts the conjecture holds. Its fetch hit a session limit and I did not read it.
events.delivers: Unverified. Per the search summary, a claim of the full conjecture; not read.
events.doubts: Not read. A claim of the full conjecture by an unknown author that has not been treated in later literature I have seen (Chamberland–Straub 2026 treat the problem as open) is a reason for doubt on its own, but I have not verified the argument.
events.direction: Claims to prove the conjecture, if accurate.

events.what_happened: Jonathan Sorenson and Jonathan Webster, 'An algorithm and computation to verify Legendre's conjecture up to 7·10^13', published in Research in Number Theory (2025). A computational check of the statement for cases up to a bound. Opened only via search summary; the exact meaning of the 7·10^13 bound (in n, or in x = n^2, or in p) is not confirmed.
events.revisions: Unknown. An earlier arXiv version may exist; not searched yet.
events.delivers: Verification of the statement for all n up to a finite bound (exact bound to be confirmed). Finite instances of a universal claim: moves no quantity the conjecture asks for, per §2.1. Used as an input in Chamberland–Straub (2026) for the RH-conditional δ ≥ 1/4 result.
events.remains: All n beyond the verified bound, i.e. the whole of problem_asks.
events.directly_checkable: The computation itself is checkable in principle; I have not read the algorithm or its implementation.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (no counterexample up to the bound); no instance of a counterexample.

events.what_happened: Ankush Goswami, 'Proof of Legendre's Conjecture', arXiv:1211.6046 (2012). The search summary quotes its abstract as claiming the result for sufficiently large n. The fetch of the PDF returned HTTP 404 and I have not read it.
events.delivers: Per the search summary, a claim for sufficiently large n only. Not checked.
events.remains: Small n in every case, and the full statement if the large-n claim is taken alone.
events.doubts: Not read. A claim of this kind has not been treated as a resolution in the sources I have seen (Wikipedia's January 2024 article and the 2026 Chamberland–Straub review do not cite it as a result).
events.direction: Claims the statement for sufficiently large n (a restricted claim), if the summary is accurate.

disputes.summary: Several unverified claims of the full conjecture exist (Sundarakannan 2019; Trushnikov 2025). None has been accepted in the sources I have read, and the 2026 review still treats the problem as open. Not resolved here.

summary: Wikipedia's article (last edited 6 January 2026, opened) lists the conjecture as open and mentions no AI. Searches show no accepted proof. The most substantive recent item is Chamberland and Straub (arXiv:2602.22502, 26 February 2026), a review of the conjecture and of RH-conditional results on primes between consecutive larger powers; it leaves the δ = 0 case, the conjecture itself, open. Sorenson and Webster's 2025 computation verifies the statement up to a finite bound (7·10^13 per the search summary; exact meaning unconfirmed), which settles no instance of a universal claim. Two claims of a full proof exist (Sundarakannan 2019; Trushnikov 2025, Russian, preprints.ru) and have not been read by me; the Trushnikov date conflicts (October 2025 per search summary, file metadata created 23 November 2025). Goswami (2012) claims only large n, from a search summary; the PDF fetch returned 404. No Lean formalisation of the conjecture itself was found; the 'legendre_QF' Lean project is about Legendre's theorem on ternary quadratic forms, a different result. No AI system has been found attributed to any mathematics on this problem. The AI search returned OpenAI-related items on other problems (unit distance conjecture; a 2026 'Human Audit of OpenAI's AI-Generated Mathematical Proofs', arXiv:2608.14673, not opened; snippet does not mention Legendre). Close call: whether the Trushnikov preprint is substantive mathematics is unknown because I could not read it.
competing_reading: Read the 2026 Chamberland–Straub result and the 2025 verification as progress on the problem (their RH-conditional result is a direct step toward primes near squares). This reading does not survive §2.1: the review changes an exponent, not the δ = 0 case, and a finite verification is one more instance of a universal claim. The Trushnikov claim, if correct, would resolve the problem outright; it is not yet read.
what_would_settle_it: Reading the Trushnikov preprint (preprints.ru/files/2520 and 2382) and checking whether its argument is complete; finding any later citation or refutation; confirming whether an AI system was used in any of these.
